input: Get a biomechanics assessment before my next marathon

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The marathon date sets a hard deadline — how much time is left determines urgency and how many follow-up sessions could realistically fit before race day.

Biomechanics assessments vary widely — a basic gait analysis at a running store is very different from a full lab-based motion-capture session with force plates. Knowing the depth required shapes where to look.
The right provider depends on the user's situation — a sports physio, a podiatrist, a running coach, or a specialist sports science lab each serves different needs.
Location determines which providers are accessible — in-person clinics vs. remote/video options, and what's realistically available nearby.
The immediate next action differs depending on whether the user already has a provider in mind, needs to research options, or needs a referral from a GP or coach.
The user may have a specific concern driving this — injury prevention, improving efficiency, correcting a known issue — which would change what to prioritise in the assessment.
What the user wants to walk away with — a report, corrective exercises, new orthotics, a coaching plan — determines whether a given assessment provider is the right fit.

gold.taskTitle: Get a biomechanics assessment before next marathon
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to schedule and complete a biomechanics assessment in preparation for an upcoming marathon.

questions.title: When exactly is your next marathon?
questions.description: The marathon date is the hard deadline for this task. Knowing it determines how urgently the assessment needs to be booked and whether there is time to act on the findings before race day.

questions.title: What depth of assessment are you looking for?
questions.description: Options range from a free treadmill gait scan at a running shop to a full lab-based motion-capture session. Clarifying this narrows down the right type of provider to target.

questions.title: What type of professional do you want to see?
questions.description: The ideal assessor could be a sports physiotherapist, podiatrist, biomechanist, or specialist running coach. The user may already have a preference or a prior relationship with one.

questions.title: Where are you based, or do you need remote options?
questions.description: Location determines which clinics or labs are accessible and whether an in-person or video-based assessment is needed.

questions.title: Do you already have a provider in mind, or need to find one?
questions.description: If the user has a clinic or practitioner in mind, the next step is simply booking. If not, research and shortlisting come first.

questions.title: What specific concern is driving this assessment?
questions.description: The user may be motivated by a recurring injury, inefficient running form, a previous assessment recommendation, or general performance optimisation. This shapes what to focus on.

questions.title: What do you want to walk away from the assessment with?
questions.description: Success could mean a written report, a set of corrective drills, custom orthotics, or a revised training plan. Knowing the desired output ensures the chosen provider can actually deliver it.
